Kuruman

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Once the

Unique Selling Point:
Kuruman in the Northern Cape is a small town with a lot of history and character. It used to be a bustling tourist destination with a thriving farming and mining community... but over the past 15 years this has all changed. The town is in disrepair, the one-of-a kind natural spring is threatened by sewage pollution, unemployment is high and crime is rife... What went wrong and is there still a chance to save this former jewel on the edge of the Kalahari?

Summary:
As you drive through the Northern Cape with its changing landscapes, it is easy to dismiss the small forgotten towns. We simply label them as one-horse towns without a Woolies Food and fibre internet… backwards…

Ons such town is Kuruman.
The town itself has a population of 13,000 people, but the local Ga-Segonyana Municipality encompasses about 75,000 people. The main source of income is farming, mining and hunting. But as the gateway to the Kalahari, the town also relies heavily on tourism.

The main tourist attraction is a natural spring - the Eye of Kuruman - which delivers about 20 to 30 million litres of crystal clear fresh water per day! it is the biggest natural spring in the southern hemisphere. The water is the lifeblood of the community, feeding the town and the Kuruman river. This is why Kuruman is also know as the Oasis of the Kalahari. The spring is also home to a variety of fish, including an endangered ciclid… Not to mention the abundant birdlife that relies on this constant supply of water.

The town has a rich history because of the natural spring. Established in 1820 when Robert Moffat built a mission station here and it was labelled as “The fountain of Christianity". And it was here where Moffat translated the Bible into Tswana - the first translation of the bible into an indigenous Southern African language. This also where David Livingstone took up his first position as a missionary in 1941. And it was the home of the famous Zulu Sangoma, Credo Mutwa, who passed away in the Kuruman Hospital in March 2020.

Further information:
Lack of maintenance and upgrades to the town’s sewer line means that sewage and the local abattoir’s wastewater is ending up in the veld/wetland surrounding the spring. It’s a disgusting site and smell that is impacting on tourism and the quality of life of the residents of Kuruman. For 8 years sludge has been spilling into the veld, just 50m from the spring and 10m from some of the houses. And it’s just a matter of time before the waste starts seeping into the underground water supply. Once this water is contaminated, there will be no turning back and the town will disappear.

And like so many other small towns, there is vast unemployment and crime is a huge problem.

— I propose a story about the town, looking at the history and the people who live there. A town that has gone from a jewel on the edge of the Kalahari, to a run-down forgotten dorpie… where people are drowning in sewage and waste, crippled by mismanagement and crime…

Stats SA says you have a 1 in 3 chance to become a victim of violent crime in Kuruman. According to residents, there have been weekly attacks on citizens by gangs of juveniles armed with knives and pipes. The picture attached is the latest attack late last week, the gentleman simply went to Midas and was attacked when he came out. The week before that a 94 year old farmer was attacked in a shopping mall. He is still fighting for his life in hospital. Nigerians have moved into the town, and are supplying an abundance of drugs to the unemployed youth. Residents say they even rip open car doors while you’re driving through the town. On Women’s Day, there was a break-in at a major retailer and stock to the value of R600k was stolen. The town is falling apart and people are desperate for help.

They also accuse the police of corruption, perpetrators are rarely arrested and official cases are seldom opened.

Accommodation 3x Nights
Travel to Kuruman
Additional presenter days

Script:



KURUMAN - a traumatised community


V/O
The N14 - a 1200km stretch of road that runs all the way from Gauteng to Spingbok in the Northern Cape. Perfect for a road trip!
UPSOUND
A roadtrip or roadie is never complete without a stop at a padstal… Well, no pepper steak pies but the search will continue…
V/O
We’re on our way to Kuruman, a small town with a big - and increasingly dubious - reputation!

BREATHER

V/O
It is images like these that draw us to the edge of the Kalahari – and not so much the search for pepper steak pies!

We want to see first hand what has become of the town that was once a firm favourite with tourists to these parts…
Braam
Once it was a beautiful town. You could walk anywhere by day, by night… everywhere where you want to go. Now you can’t even go out of your house…
V/O
Braam van der Westhuizen has lived here for over three decades and will be our guide for the next couple of days.

BREATHER

V/o
On top of running his own businesses, he’s also taken on the role of Ward Councillor, which appears to be a full-time job…
Braam
Sometimes you receive between 800 and 2000 messages per day…

Derek: So what do you see as the main problems here?

For the past 26 years the infrastructure of this town was neglected. We do not have enough electricity. The water is a problem and the sewer is a bigger problem.
V/O
Water leaks, defunct sewage pump stations and mountains of litter tell the story of a small town that has grown exponentially, while the ailing infrastructure has been unable to keep up with the demand.

Our first stop is the town treasure - a natural spring, known as the largest in the Southern hemisphere.

We’re joined by former resident, Willie Aucamp.
Willie & Derek
Derek: So this is the Oog?

Willie: Die Kuruman Oog. A place that used to be known as the Oasis of the Kalahari…
V/O
Here some 20 million litres of crystal clear water bubbles to the surface every single day.
LINK
The Eye of Kuruman was discovered in 1801 - a truly magnificent natural spring providing a haven for birdlife and even some endangered fish. Now, a cesspool of filth…
V/O
And everywhere … reminders of the town's other major challenge. One ﻿we'll later have a brush with ourselves. For now, we continue our visit to The Eye in the company of 2 security guards.
Willie
Willie: If you reach with your hand you’ll be able to drink it. It’s clean fresh underground water that comes out of the earth.

Derek: So we can take a swim there?

Willie: You can take a swim there but not 100m from there.


V/O
Having lived in Kuruman for many years, Willie now represents the Kalahari constituency in Parliament.
Willie
The problem is right across the road, about 100m from here where it flows into the Kuruman river the water that you see here that’s clean and crystal, immediately becomes contaminated.
V/O
From here, the water is supposed to be channelled through town, some 40kms north to neighbouring communities.


Willie
This is the water flowing out from underneath the road…
Willie
Willie: If you go downstream from here, further on, the more the contamination gets, and the less usable this water becomes…
V/O
In this building someone installed a toilet with no linkage to the town’s sewage system and the raw waste simply washes into the channel.

And on a daily basis, failing pump stations throughout town add to the sewage load in the water.
Willie
Children play on this water. They get sick. It’s totally unacceptable and the solution is not difficult. Clean up the riverbed and maintain it once it’s been done…
V/O
All the way through town and beyond the channels are blocked with litter, sludge and reeds… so most of the water simply dams up, creating large and smelly sewage swamps throughout the suburbs…

V/O
This is a local primary school that has been flooded since March this year.
Nadia
Willie: And this is your soccer field…

Yes, and all the way at the back it’s more than knee-height …
V/O
Nadia Myburg is a teacher here at the Kuruman Tuition Centre. They’ve spent thousands of rands trying to keep the contaminated water out.
Nadia
We tried everything. We built walls, ground walls. We even drove in gravel. It didn’t work. It only lasted a while then the water came back.
V/O
It’s time for lunch and we stop at a local coffee shop. While we escape the ever-present sewage smell for a few minutes, we’re reminded that dirty water is not the only problem in Kuruman.
UPSOUND
Drilling
V/O
There have been three break-ins here in recent weeks and security is being beefed up. Everyone you talk to has a story to tell…
Marelize
Ek het die fietse agter op die bakkie gesit en vasgestrap. En so het ek in die dorp ingery.

I put the bikes on the back of the bakkie and strapped them down, and I drove into town like that.
V/O
Marelize Viviers runs a lodge just outside of town, and should’ve known better when she decided to drive down the main street of Kuruman with two expensive bicycles on the back of her bakkie.
Marelize
Toe spring daar 3 mense op die bakkie en hulle trek aan die fietse. En ek dog hier’s ek nou in die moeilikheid. Ek het op die briek getrap, die klomp het vorentoe gegaan in die bakkie en die volgende oomblik besluit ek nou moet ek hier wegry. En ek trap toe die petrol en af is hulle van die bakkie af. Maar sjoe, het ek geskrik… dit was verskriklik gewees!

Then three people jumped on the back of the bakkie and tugged at the bikes. Then I thought now I’m in trouble. I hit the brakes. The guys fell forward on the bakkie and the next moment I decided I must drive away. Then I stepped on the petrol and they fell off. But, sjoe, did I get a fright! It was terrible.
V/o
But underneath the smiles and lighthearted anecdotes lies a deeply traumatised community…
Braam
It’s a daunting task to go and do shopping and actually survive it.

Derek: So, it’s like Survivor Kuruman?

Ja, for sure.


V/O
We stop off at another one of the town’s tourist attractions… After all, we’ve come all this way… might as well do a little sightseeing…
LINK
Apart from present day problems, Kuruman has a rich history. This is the Moffat Mission about 5 minutes out of town. And just one of Robert Moffat’s many achievements was translating the bible into setswana… no mean feat in the early 1800’s…
V/O
The mission still houses the original printing press that Moffat used.
V/O
Today, Kuruman is a very different place. The town is run by the Ga-Segonyana Local Municipality and we head to their offices to meet with Municipal Manager, Martin Tsatsimpe.
Martin
Derek: First of all, congratulations… you are one of the first Municipal Managers prepared to speak to us on camera…

Martin: oh, thank you so much…
V/O
Tsatimpe is quick to admit that there are serious problems with the town’s service delivery.
Martin
If you look how it’s been designed and the growth, the development… we’re lagging behind in terms of augmenting the bulk infrastructure or sewer.

Derek: Like Pumpstations?

Pumpstations as well. Pipes are very small. Most of them have been installed 2 decades ago.
V/O
But apparently the problems are being addressed. They’re building a water reservoir, the Eye will be refurbished and plans to clean up the town are well underway.
Martin
We already started the operation of eliminating or taking out all the car washes along the eye. We started a week ago. There’s still resistance. We brought in SAPS. but yes, …

Derek: We thought it was because Carte Blanche was coming to town…

No, no no. if you look at, we’ve been engaging… we actually started 2 months ago, also evicting unlawful people around town…
V/O
But this was us… just one day earlier … and not a single sign that these types of activities are being discouraged…

Illegal car washes, however, are the least of Kuruman’s problems…
Zukile
I used to work in Joburg. In Joburg, crime like this is not like this…
V/O
Zukile Vumazonke has worked here as a private security guard for about 4 years. He’s fed up with the lack of efficient law enforcement in town.
Zukile
Those Tsotsis are always outside. Even if you report them at the police station after 2 days you see that guy who was robbing someone…


V/O
And the perpetrators will not hesitate to use violence.
Braam
They come in gangs of 6 to 12, they attack you, they will assault you with knives.
V/O
And these incidents happen on a daily basis. In fact, there was a robbery right here in the parking lot less than an hour after we left…
Woman

Just yesterday on that corner over there a bunch of young boys robbed a girl of her phone.


V/O
It’s difficult finding people in town willing to speak out about the ongoing crime…
Woman
I am scared. Even now I'm scared. You can hear them intimidating me and swearing at me.
V/O
In the blink of an eye the situation turns precarious…

UPSOUND: Why do you talk shit to these whites? You should sleep with these whites.

We’re surrounded by a group of angry young men, most likely trying to distract us so they can make a quick getaway with our cameras.

All this on the doorstep of the local police station.

Even the Municipal Manager has had enough!
Martin
We need the involvement and the presence of the South African police because they are mandated constitutionally to make arrest and all that. But we are saying that this must be a collaborative effort.
Derek: Are they not active enough?
I will not speak on behalf of SAPS, but the crime stats talk for themselves.
Derek: I mean, these attacks seem to be on a daily basis just with cell phones and wallets. You must be worried.
We are worried as a municipality because. We'll never have an investor come into Kuruman when their investment is not secure.


V/O
Tsatsimpe believes the tide is turning and great improvements are planned for Kuruman. And the Northern Cape Provincial Police say they have put measures in place to address the crime. But, I guess only time will tell if this will make a real difference in the lives of the people of Kuruman…








PROMO 1 11”
Ailing infrastructure, alleged mismanagement and rampant crime… some of the issues plaguing Kuruman in the Northern Cape. But is there enough money and heart to turn the town around?




PROMO 2 21”
UPSOUND: People have been mugged, it’s a fact. People have been killed. Tourists are scared.

It’s a small town with a big reputation. Kuruman in the Northern Cape is a cesspool of filth and criminals…

UPSOUND: They come in gangs of 6 to 12. They attack you. Assault you with knives…

What has become of the Oasis of the Kalahari?




PROMO 3 21”
Over 20 million litres of crystal clear spring water gushing to the surface every single day.

UPSOUND: Derek: So this is the Oog?

Willie: Die Kuruman Oog. A place that used to be known as the Oasis of the Kalahari…

But this water is of no value to anyone…

UPSOUND: Children play on this water. They get sick. It’s totally unacceptable.

We put the spotlight on Kuruman in the Northern Cape…

UPSOUND Drilling V/O There have been three break-ins here in recent weeks and security is being beefed up. Everyone you talk to has a story to tell… Marelize Ek het die fietse agter op die bakkie gesit en vasgestrap. En so het ek in die dorp ingery. I put the bikes on the back of the bakkie and strapped them down, and I drove into town like that. V/O Marelize Viviers runs a lodge just outside of town, and should’ve known better when she decided to drive down the main street of Kuruman with two expensive bicycles on the back of her bakkie. Marelize Toe spring daar 3 mense op die bakkie en hulle trek aan die fietse. En ek dog hier’s ek nou in die moeilikheid. Ek het op die briek getrap, die klomp het vorentoe gegaan in die bakkie en die volgende oomblik besluit ek nou moet ek hier wegry. En ek trap toe die petrol en af is hulle van die bakkie af. Maar sjoe, het ek geskrik… dit was verskriklik gewees! Then three people jumped on the back of the bakkie and tugged at the bikes. Then I thought now I’m in trouble. I hit the brakes. The guys fell forward on the bakkie and the next moment I decided I must drive away. Then I stepped on the petrol and they fell off. But, sjoe, did I get a fright! It was terrible. V/o But underneath the smiles and lighthearted anecdotes lies a deeply traumatised community… Braam It’s a daunting task to go and do shopping and actually survive it. Derek: So, it’s like Survivor Kuruman? Ja, for sure. V/O We stop off at another one of the town’s tourist attractions… After all, we’ve come all this way… might as well do a little sightseeing… LINK Apart from present day problems, Kuruman has a rich history. This is the Moffat Mission about 5 minutes out of town. And just one of Robert Moffat’s many achievements was translating the bible into setswana… no mean feat in the early 1800’s… V/O The mission still houses the original printing press that Moffat used. V/O Today, Kuruman is a very different place. The town is run by the Ga-Segonyana Local Municipality and we head to their offices to meet with Municipal Manager, Martin Tsatsimpe. Martin Derek: First of all, congratulations… you are one of the first Municipal Managers prepared to speak to us on camera… Martin: oh, thank you so much… V/O Tsatimpe is quick to admit that there are serious problems with the town’s service delivery. Martin If you look how it’s been designed and the growth, the development… we’re lagging behind in terms of augmenting the bulk infrastructure or sewer. Derek: Like Pumpstations? Pumpstations as well. Pipes are very small. Most of them have been installed 2 decades ago. V/O But apparently the problems are being addressed. They’re building a water reservoir, the Eye will be refurbished and plans to clean up the town are well underway. Martin We already started the operation of eliminating or taking out all the car washes along the eye. We started a week ago. There’s still resistance. We brought in SAPS. but yes, … Derek: We thought it was because Carte Blanche was coming to town… No, no no. if you look at, we’ve been engaging… we actually started 2 months ago, also evicting unlawful people around town… V/O But this was us… just one day earlier … and not a single sign that these types of activities are being discouraged… Illegal car washes, however, are the least of Kuruman’s problems… Zukile I used to work in Joburg. In Joburg, crime like this is not like this… V/O Zukile Vumazonke has worked here as a private security guard for about 4 years. He’s fed up with the lack of efficient law enforcement in town. Zukile Those Tsotsis are always outside. Even if you report them at the police station after 2 days you see that guy who was robbing someone… V/O And the perpetrators will not hesitate to use violence. Braam They come in gangs of 6 to 12, they attack you, they will assault you with knives. V/O And these incidents happen on a daily basis. In fact, there was a robbery right here in the parking lot less than an hour after we left… Woman Just yesterday on that corner over there a bunch of young boys robbed a girl of her phone. V/O It’s difficult finding people in town willing to speak out about the ongoing crime… Woman I am scared. Even now I'm scared. You can hear them intimidating me and swearing at me. V/O In the blink of an eye the situation turns precarious… UPSOUND: Why do you talk shit to these whites? You should sleep with these whites. We’re surrounded by a group of angry young men, most likely trying to distract us so they can make a quick getaway with our cameras. All this on the doorstep of the local police station. Even the Municipal Manager has had enough! Martin We need the involvement and the presence of the South African police because they are mandated constitutionally to make arrest and all that. But we are saying that this must be a collaborative effort. Derek: Are they not active enough? I will not speak on behalf of SAPS, but the crime stats talk for themselves. Derek: I mean, these attacks seem to be on a daily basis just with cell phones and wallets. You must be worried. We are worried as a municipality because. We'll never have an investor come into Kuruman when their investment is not secure. V/O Tsatsimpe believes the tide is turning and great improvements are planned for Kuruman. And the Northern Cape Provincial Police say they have put measures in place to address the crime. But, I guess only time will tell if this will make a real difference in the lives of the people of Kuruman… PROMO 1 11” Ailing infrastructure, alleged mismanagement and rampant crime… some of the issues plaguing Kuruman in the Northern Cape. But is there enough money and heart to turn the town around? PROMO 2 21” UPSOUND: People have been mugged, it’s a fact. People have been killed. Tourists are scared. It’s a small town with a big reputation. Kuruman in the Northern Cape is a cesspool of filth and criminals… UPSOUND: They come in gangs of 6 to 12. They attack you. Assault you with knives… What has become of the Oasis of the Kalahari? PROMO 3 21” Over 20 million litres of crystal clear spring water gushing to the surface every single day. UPSOUND: Derek: So this is the Oog? Willie: Die Kuruman Oog. A place that used to be known as the Oasis of the Kalahari… But this water is of no value to anyone… UPSOUND: Children play on this water. They get sick. It’s totally unacceptable. We put the spotlight on Kuruman in the Northern Cape…

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Kuruman in the Northern Cape is a small town with a lot of history and character. It used to be a bustling tourist destination with a thriving farming and mining community... but over the past 15 years this has all changed. The town is in disrepair, the one-of-a kind natural spring is threatened by sewage pollution, unemployment is high and crime is rife... What went wrong and is there still a chance to save this former jewel on the edge of the Kalahari?
metadata.Summary: As you drive through the Northern Cape with its changing landscapes, it is easy to dismiss the small forgotten towns. We simply label them as one-horse towns without a Woolies Food and fibre internet… backwards… Ons such town is Kuruman. The town itself has a population of 13,000 people, but the local Ga-Segonyana Municipality encompasses about 75,000 people. The main source of income is farming, mining and hunting. But as the gateway to the Kalahari, the town also relies heavily on tourism. The main tourist attraction is a natural spring - the Eye of Kuruman - which delivers about 20 to 30 million litres of crystal clear fresh water per day! it is the biggest natural spring in the southern hemisphere. The water is the lifeblood of the community, feeding the town and the Kuruman river. This is why Kuruman is also know as the Oasis of the Kalahari. The spring is also home to a variety of fish, including an endangered ciclid… Not to mention the abundant birdlife that relies on this constant supply of water. The town has a rich history because of the natural spring. Established in 1820 when Robert Moffat built a mission station here and it was labelled as “The fountain of Christianity". And it was here where Moffat translated the Bible into Tswana - the first translation of the bible into an indigenous Southern African language. This also where David Livingstone took up his first position as a missionary in 1941. And it was the home of the famous Zulu Sangoma, Credo Mutwa, who passed away in the Kuruman Hospital in March 2020.
metadata.Further information: Lack of maintenance and upgrades to the town’s sewer line means that sewage and the local abattoir’s wastewater is ending up in the veld/wetland surrounding the spring. It’s a disgusting site and smell that is impacting on tourism and the quality of life of the residents of Kuruman. For 8 years sludge has been spilling into the veld, just 50m from the spring and 10m from some of the houses. And it’s just a matter of time before the waste starts seeping into the underground water supply. Once this water is contaminated, there will be no turning back and the town will disappear. And like so many other small towns, there is vast unemployment and crime is a huge problem. — I propose a story about the town, looking at the history and the people who live there. A town that has gone from a jewel on the edge of the Kalahari, to a run-down forgotten dorpie… where people are drowning in sewage and waste, crippled by mismanagement and crime… Stats SA says you have a 1 in 3 chance to become a victim of violent crime in Kuruman. According to residents, there have been weekly attacks on citizens by gangs of juveniles armed with knives and pipes. The picture attached is the latest attack late last week, the gentleman simply went to Midas and was attacked when he came out. The week before that a 94 year old farmer was attacked in a shopping mall. He is still fighting for his life in hospital. Nigerians have moved into the town, and are supplying an abundance of drugs to the unemployed youth. Residents say they even rip open car doors while you’re driving through the town. On Women’s Day, there was a break-in at a major retailer and stock to the value of R600k was stolen. The town is falling apart and people are desperate for help. They also accuse the police of corruption, perpetrators are rarely arrested and official cases are seldom opened.
